After the printer

The step that was missing.

Everything before your printer has an owner and a process. Everything after it is improvised. Pages are gathered, arranged, punched, stapled, slid into a folder, and sent out.

CDIS is the step that was missing. In about ninety seconds it seals a printed document into a proper hard cover record that holds together for decades and shows visible physical damage if anyone opens it or changes a page. The printed page may be a court filing, an executed agreement, a compiled record or an archive. It may pass through many hands and be required again years later.

CDIS gives that last step a standard: an installed, written, trained way of finishing the official paper records an organisation produces every day.

A question before anything elseDoes your office have printers? Nobody prints for fun. You print the things that have to be signed, stamped, sealed, and handed to somebody.

The finished record

Five things a record should be.

  1. Sealed.

    The printed pages become one finished record in a proper hard cover, closed on a steel spine with a thermal seal.

  2. Tamper evident.

    Opening the sealed record or changing a page leaves visible physical damage. The document can answer for itself.

  3. Presented.

    The document reaches its recipient as a finished, book quality record, with a cover chosen for its purpose.

  4. Repeatable.

    A written house standard gives every trained user the same way to finish the record, in every office.

  5. Preservable.

    The hard cover record holds together for decades of handling and retention, and is archived in the state it was presented.

Where it matters

Four kinds of document carry this exposure.

Court filings and official submissions

The record leaves your office to be filed, served or submitted. Its recipient judges the document they receive.

Compiled records handled for years

The same record passes through many hands over a long proceeding or retention period. It has to hold together when it is produced again.

Title documents and executed agreements

The client takes the document away and keeps it for decades. The finished record has to survive beyond your control.

The archive

The organisation is obliged to be able to produce the record. Retention begins with the way that record is finished.

The case law behind this exposure, and what it costs to carry it, is set out on the evidence page.

The CDIS configurations

Three configurations. One standard.

Each configuration is built on a Peleman UniBinder system and produces the same sealed, tamper evident record. The difference is capacity and throughput.

Configuration and investment are confirmed after a free thirty minute workflow assessment, because the right system depends on your record volume, thickness, copies, users and locations.
